interview_metadata.name: Keith Moore
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) - Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born in Mesa, Arizona, in 1966, and I grew up around Apache Junction before it got as built up as it is now. My dad worked as a mechanic and my mom worked a few years at a school cafeteria, so our house was practical, plain, and everybody fixed what they had instead of replacing it. I was never a big school person, but I did fine through high school and liked shop class, engines, electrical basics, and anything where you could see the result in your hands. After high school I worked construction, appliance repair, odd-job maintenance, and then handyman work for a long stretch. I married my wife, Linda, in my late twenties, and we raised two kids, both grown now. The biggest parts of my life have been learning to make myself useful, staying close to family, and staying tied to the desert. In the last few years I stopped doing paid handyman work and started leading workshops at the senior center, mostly home maintenance, tool safety, small engine basics, and little woodworking projects.

follow_ups.question: What was your childhood home like day to day?
follow_ups.response: It was modest and busy. Weekdays meant school, chores, and helping Dad hold a flashlight while he fixed a truck or a swamp cooler. Weekends we might drive out near the Superstitions or visit relatives in the Phoenix area.

follow_ups.question: When did you first realize you were good with repairs?
follow_ups.response: Probably around fourteen or fifteen. A neighbor had an old mower that would not start, and Dad showed me how to clean the carburetor. When it fired up, that stuck with me.

follow_ups.question: Who has been most central in your adult life?
follow_ups.response: Linda first, then my kids and grandkids. I have friends from the senior center, ATV riding, and cards, but my family is the anchor.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: A big crossroads was when I decided to quit chasing bigger construction jobs around the Valley and stay closer to Apache Junction doing repair and handyman work. I was in my thirties, the kids were little, and I could have made more money taking longer jobs farther out. But Linda and I were both tired of me leaving before sunrise and getting home worn out. I started taking smaller jobs nearby: appliances, cabinets, leaks, fans, doors, little electrical fixes. It was not fancy, but people trusted me, and I could coach Little League, get to school events, and still keep food on the table. That choice made me more community-rooted than career-ladder-minded.

follow_ups.question: Was that financially scary?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially the first year. We kept a notebook budget, drove used vehicles, and I said yes to a lot of small jobs that added up.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone influence that decision?
follow_ups.response: Linda did, in a steady way. She never gave me an ultimatum, but she asked what kind of father I wanted to be, and that landed.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: That one was a conscious choice. I sat down with Linda at the kitchen table and we ran the numbers, then I told a contractor I was not going to follow the next job out of town.

follow_ups.question: Do you remember how you felt after deciding?
follow_ups.response: Nervous, but lighter. I knew the money might be tighter, but I also knew I would be home.

follow_ups.question: Did the decision change how you saw yourself?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I stopped measuring myself by the size of the job and started measuring by whether people could count on me.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Some small-business guidance would have helped. I learned pricing, taxes, and scheduling by trial and error, and I made a few mistakes early on.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have mattered most?
follow_ups.response: Basic bookkeeping and how to bid jobs without undercutting myself.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone eventually help you learn that?
follow_ups.response: An older plumber named Walt showed me how he wrote estimates and kept receipts in order.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am married to Linda, and we have been married a little over thirty years. She is steady, organized, and more patient than I am. We have two adult children. Our son, Brian, lives in Mesa and works in HVAC, and our daughter, Erin, lives outside Tucson and works at a dental office. Between them we have four grandkids, and I try to be the grandpa who teaches them how to use a screwdriver, read a trail sign, and not panic when something breaks. We do Sunday dinners a couple times a month, and I video call the grandkids when they want help with a project or just want to show me something.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your children?
follow_ups.response: Brian we see every week or two because Mesa is close. Erin is more like once a month in person, with calls and texts in between.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Linda usually do together?
follow_ups.response: We take evening walks, watch Diamondbacks or Suns games, go to local theater now and then, and plan short road trips when the budget allows.

follow_ups.question: What are you teaching your grandchildren lately?
follow_ups.response: One grandson is learning to sand and stain a small shelf. One granddaughter likes birdhouses, so we have been painting those and talking about desert birds.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: I have a younger sister, Marlene, in New Mexico. We talk every couple weeks and trade family updates, but we do not see each other as much as I would like.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you connected with her?
follow_ups.response: Mostly phone calls and old family stories. She remembers details I forget.

follow_ups.question: Do you visit her?
follow_ups.response: Once a year if the truck is behaving and we can work it into a road trip.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: I have a few close friends from the senior center and community hall. There is Walt, who is older than me and still sharper than most people with tools. There is Mike, who rides ATVs with me, and Ray, who plays cards on Thursday nights. I would not call myself a huge social butterfly, but I like having people I can count on and people who can count on me.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see these friends?
follow_ups.response: Usually two or three times a week between workshops, cards, and occasional rides.

follow_ups.question: What do you talk about together?
follow_ups.response: Repairs, family, sports, local politics, trail conditions, and who made a bad play in the card game.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We live in Apache Junction, not too far from the Superstition Mountains, in a quiet older neighborhood with single-story homes, gravel yards, cactus, mesquite, and a few RVs. People here are practical. You see neighbors out early before the heat hits, watering desert plants, walking dogs, or tinkering in garages. It is not fancy, but it suits me. I like seeing the mountains change color in the evening, and I like that if somebody's gate breaks, three people know how to fix it.

follow_ups.question: Who do you know nearby?
follow_ups.response: I know the folks on both sides, a widow across the street, and a retired couple two houses down. We trade tools and keep an eye on each other's places.

follow_ups.question: What is a typical morning like on your street?
follow_ups.response: Quiet. By six-thirty you hear garage doors, birds, and maybe someone starting a truck before the day gets hot.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel pretty safe. We have occasional petty theft, mostly unlocked cars or tools left out, but neighbors watch out and most trouble is avoided with common sense.

follow_ups.question: Do you take any precautions?
follow_ups.response: I lock the shed, keep lights working, and do not leave tools visible in the truck.

follow_ups.question: Do neighbors communicate about safety?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly by texts or just walking over. Nothing formal, but it works.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The ups are the desert, the slower pace, and the people. The downs are summer heat, rising costs, traffic from growth, and sometimes folks not respecting trails or leaving trash.

follow_ups.question: What change bothers you most?
follow_ups.response: The growth without enough thought. More houses, more traffic, and not always enough respect for the land.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you there?
follow_ups.response: The mountains, family nearby, and the sense that I still belong here.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: It is just me and Linda in the house full time. We have a two-bedroom place with a garage that is half workshop, half storage. The grandkids stay over sometimes, usually one or two at a time, but nobody else lives here.

follow_ups.question: How do you divide household responsibilities?
follow_ups.response: Linda handles more scheduling and paperwork. I handle repairs, yard work, vehicle maintenance, and a lot of the grilling.

follow_ups.question: What space in the house is most yours?
follow_ups.response: The garage workbench. That is where the tools, birdhouse supplies, and small engine parts live.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is permanent. It is just me and Linda.

follow_ups.question: No one staying short term right now?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now.

follow_ups.question: Do guests stay often?
follow_ups.response: Only family, and only for a night or two.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Grandkids sometimes stay on weekends, and my sister has stayed during visits.

follow_ups.question: How often do the grandkids sleep over?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once a month, more during school breaks.

follow_ups.question: Where do guests sleep?
follow_ups.response: The spare room, unless the grandkids decide the living room is more fun.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody who usually lives here is away.

follow_ups.question: No college student or traveling relative tied to the household?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Has that happened recently?
follow_ups.response: No, not in recent years.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: I get up around 5:30 or 6:00 most mornings, earlier in summer so I can beat the heat. Mondays and Wednesdays I usually work in the garage or garden. Tuesdays I lead a workshop at the senior center, usually from about 9:00 to 11:30. Thursdays I play cards in the evening at the community hall. Fridays I might hike early or run errands with Linda. Weekends are family, ATV riding if I have one scheduled, a golf outing once in a while, or watching the Diamondbacks.

follow_ups.question: What does a workshop day look like?
follow_ups.response: I load tools by 7:45, get to the center before 8:30, set up benches and safety gear, teach, then clean up and talk with whoever has questions.

follow_ups.question: When do you usually exercise?
follow_ups.response: Early morning. I hike or walk before the heat, and I stretch in the evening if my back is tight.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I am not in the workforce now. I used to do handyman and repair work, but I am retired from paid jobs. What I do now is volunteer workshop leading at the senior center, and I sometimes help neighbors with small repairs, but I do not charge like a business anymore. I try to keep that to a manageable amount because I do not want retirement to turn back into full-time work.

follow_ups.question: How many hours a week do you volunteer?
follow_ups.response: Usually five to eight hours when you count prep, teaching, and cleaning up.

follow_ups.question: Do neighbors try to pay you?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes. I usually tell them to cover parts or bring brisket meat, coffee, or just pay it forward.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I keep the household maintenance schedule, take care of the desert landscaping, and manage our vehicle upkeep. I also track our budget every Sunday evening. Linda and I share grocery shopping, and I cook dinner two or three nights a week, usually something grilled or southwestern.

follow_ups.question: What does your Sunday budgeting involve?
follow_ups.response: I check the bank account, receipts, upcoming bills, and what we spent on gas, groceries, and prescriptions.

follow_ups.question: What yard work do you do?
follow_ups.response: Trimming cactus pads, checking drip lines, clearing weeds, and keeping native shrubs from getting wild.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: I have slowed down the heavy lifting this past year because my right knee and lower back complain if I act like I am thirty. I also added more workshop planning because the senior center asked me to do a basic electronics series. Linda and I have been walking more in the evenings because her doctor encouraged it and it helps both of us sleep.

follow_ups.question: What did you cut back on?
follow_ups.response: Big appliance moving, roof work, and long ATV rides in extreme heat.

follow_ups.question: What changed with the electronics workshops?
follow_ups.response: I started making handouts and simple practice boards so people can learn safely.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: My children are grown, so I am not managing school routines now. My grandkids are the school-age ones. Their routines are mostly handled by their parents, but I hear about soccer practice, homework, band, and one who is getting into robotics. If I pick them up, it is usually an afternoon favor, and then they come over for snacks and maybe a small project.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with child care regularly?
follow_ups.response: Not daily, but we help when parents have appointments or work conflicts.

follow_ups.question: What activities do you enjoy doing with them after school?
follow_ups.response: Simple woodworking, checking bird feeders, and occasionally helping with science fair type projects.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My experiences have mostly been ordinary: traffic stops, accident reports, and seeing deputies around trailheads. I got a speeding ticket years ago and deserved it. Around off-road areas, I have dealt with rangers or deputies checking permits and making sure people are not tearing up closed trails. I try to keep things legal and respectful.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever felt treated unfairly by police?
follow_ups.response: Personally, no, not in a serious way. I know that is not everyone's experience.

follow_ups.question: What are law enforcement interactions like during ATV rides?
follow_ups.response: Usually quick. They check registrations, remind folks about closures, and move on if you are behaving.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: A neighbor had a shed burglary a few years back, and deputies came out. They were polite, but there was not much they could do because there were no cameras or serial numbers.

follow_ups.question: Did that change anything you do?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I wrote down tool serial numbers and put better locks on my shed.

follow_ups.question: Did neighbors talk about it?
follow_ups.response: Yes, it made everyone more careful for a while.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested. I have a cousin who had a DUI years ago, and that shook the family up, but he got through the court requirements and changed his drinking.

follow_ups.question: Was that close to you personally?
follow_ups.response: Not day to day, but family talked about it, and it was a warning to everybody.

follow_ups.question: Did it affect your own choices?
follow_ups.response: Yes. If I drink at all, I stay home or Linda drives.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote pretty much every election, especially local and state ones. I do mail-in because it gives me time to read the propositions and judges. I do not like people complaining all year and then skipping the ballot. I may not love every candidate, but I think voting is part of keeping your say.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics with others?
follow_ups.response: A little, mostly with Linda and a couple friends. I avoid turning card night into an argument.

follow_ups.question: What races do you pay closest attention to?
follow_ups.response: City issues, county offices, water, roads, taxes, public safety, and land use.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would call myself independent but leaning Republican, mostly old-style practical conservative. I care about budgets, public safety, property rights, and not wasting taxpayer money. But I am not interested in screaming politics or treating people like enemies. I think government has a role in roads, emergency services, veterans, seniors, schools, and protecting public lands from being wrecked. I get frustrated with both parties because they play to the loudest people. I want competence more than slogans. On local issues I look at who understands water, growth, and the desert, not just the letter after their name.

follow_ups.question: What does practical conservative mean to you?
follow_ups.response: Spend carefully, maintain what we build, let people live their lives, and do not promise things without a way to pay for them.

follow_ups.question: Where do you break from Republicans?
follow_ups.response: I think some ignore health care costs and environmental damage too much. Public land and water are not small issues here.

follow_ups.question: What political tone turns you off?
follow_ups.response: Name-calling and conspiracy talk. I like evidence, not people forwarding nonsense online.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have gotten less loyal to parties and more focused on whether someone can actually govern. The last few years made me tired of national politics. Locally, I have become more serious about water, heat, and growth because those affect our daily life. I still lean conservative on spending, but I am less patient with leaders who pretend problems are fake.

follow_ups.question: What issue changed your thinking most?
follow_ups.response: Water. You cannot live in Arizona and act like water planning is optional.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone influence that change?
follow_ups.response: Mostly neighbors, local meetings, and just seeing more development push into the desert.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: I would say it affected me somewhat. I am a white man in a town where my experience with police has mostly been straightforward, so I know I do not see everything. Some of what I heard made me think harder about how different people's experiences can be. I also believe most officers are trying to do a hard job, so I tend to look for reforms that improve accountability without painting everyone with one brush.

follow_ups.question: Did you follow the protests closely?
follow_ups.response: I followed them on the news and talked about them with family, but I did not attend protests.

follow_ups.question: What part stayed with you?
follow_ups.response: The idea that a routine police encounter can feel very different depending on who you are.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the core issue is whether people are treated fairly and whether bad policing is corrected. I can support better training, body cameras, clear discipline, and hiring good people. I get uneasy when the conversation turns into abolishing police completely because rural and desert communities still need emergency response. But accountability makes sense to me.

follow_ups.question: Have your views changed through family conversations?
follow_ups.response: Yes, my daughter pushes me to listen more before reacting. That has probably helped.

follow_ups.question: What reform sounds most reasonable to you?
follow_ups.response: Transparent review when force is used, and training that helps officers de-escalate.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think the country still carries a lot of history, and it shows up in schools, neighborhoods, policing, and who gets trusted. I was raised to judge people by how they act, and I still believe in that, but I also understand now that not everybody starts from the same place. I am not an expert. I try to listen, be fair, and not pretend my life explains everyone else's.

follow_ups.question: Where do you learn about these issues?
follow_ups.response: News, some documentaries Linda watches, and conversations with younger family members.

follow_ups.question: Is this discussed in your friend circle?
follow_ups.response: A little, but carefully. Some friends get defensive fast.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with family and a few friends, but I have not joined protests. Mostly I listen more than I used to and try not to jump in with a quick opinion.

follow_ups.question: Who do you talk with most about it?
follow_ups.response: Linda and Erin, because they both think things through and will challenge me respectfully.

follow_ups.question: Have you changed any behavior?
follow_ups.response: I am more careful about what I repeat online or in conversation.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Linda is thoughtful and pretty sympathetic to reform. My daughter is more outspoken about racial fairness. My son is more like me, supportive of good policing but open to accountability. Some of my older friends think the whole discussion has gone too far, so I do not push it too hard with them.

follow_ups.question: Does this cause family conflict?
follow_ups.response: Not really. We disagree sometimes, but we keep it respectful.

follow_ups.question: Do your grandchildren ask about it?
follow_ups.response: The older ones do, mostly from school or things they see online.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I am in decent health for sixty. I have mild high blood pressure, a stiff lower back, and a right knee that reminds me not to overdo it. I try to stay active with walking, hiking, yard work, and lighter woodworking. I am not trying to be twenty-five, but I want to stay independent as long as I can.

follow_ups.question: Do you take regular medication?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a low-dose blood pressure medication, plus occasional ibuprofen if my doctor says it is okay.

follow_ups.question: What health goal matters most?
follow_ups.response: Keeping mobility. If I can walk trails and work at my bench, I feel like myself.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: The easy part is that I like being outdoors and active, so exercise does not feel like punishment. The hard part is Arizona heat, aches from old work, and good food costing more than it used to. Also, brisket is not exactly health food, even if I make a good one.

follow_ups.question: How do you handle summer heat?
follow_ups.response: I do everything early, drink water, wear a hat, and stop before pride gets me in trouble.

follow_ups.question: What foods do you try to choose?
follow_ups.response: More grilled vegetables, beans, chicken, cactus paddles, salsa, and less fried food.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: The main thing was my doctor telling me my blood pressure needed attention, so I started medication and got more serious about walking. I also had a knee flare-up after an ATV event last fall. Nothing broken, but it swelled up and forced me to rest, ice it, and accept that I need knee supports and better pacing.

follow_ups.question: Did the knee change your activities?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I shortened hikes and stopped doing rough rides back to back.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see a doctor?
follow_ups.response: At least twice a year now, plus labs when they want to check things.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: They affect what I take on, but I am not disabled. I avoid heavy jobs and ask for help lifting. Since I am retired, I can pace myself better than when I was doing paid repair work.

follow_ups.question: What tasks are harder now?
follow_ups.response: Crawling under sinks, carrying appliances, roofing, and kneeling too long.

follow_ups.question: Do you use tools to adapt?
follow_ups.response: Yes, dollies, clamps, knee pads, and a rule that I do not lift stupid anymore.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Linda has some arthritis in her hands and one hip, so I worry about her comfort. My sister had a cancer scare that turned out okay after treatment, and that made me pay more attention to checkups. We are at the age where health news comes up more often at the family table.

follow_ups.question: Do you help Linda with daily tasks?
follow_ups.response: I open stubborn jars, handle heavy laundry baskets, and do more of the yard work.

follow_ups.question: Did your sister's illness change family contact?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I called more often and visited when she was recovering.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We get care, but insurance is expensive and confusing. Since I am sixty and not on Medicare yet, we use a marketplace plan, and Linda has some coverage through part-time work but not enough to make everything simple. I have delayed dental work before because the quote was high. I have not skipped urgent care, but I do ask what things cost.

follow_ups.question: What care have you delayed?
follow_ups.response: A crown and some follow-up physical therapy for my knee. I did exercises at home instead.

follow_ups.question: How far do you travel for care?
follow_ups.response: Usually Mesa or east Valley clinics, about twenty to forty minutes depending on traffic.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Nothing too far out. We use heat, ice, stretching, Epsom salt soaks, and herbal teas when someone has a cold. Linda tried acupuncture once for hip pain and said it helped some. I respect home remedies, but if something is serious I want a real doctor involved.

follow_ups.question: Any desert plants used medicinally?
follow_ups.response: Aloe for minor burns, but I am careful. I do not mess with plants unless I know what they are.

follow_ups.question: Who taught you those remedies?
follow_ups.response: Mostly my mother and older neighbors.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I drink occasionally, usually a beer while grilling or watching a game, but not every day. When I am stressed, I am more likely to go to the garage, sand a board, sharpen tools, or take a walk. Drinking never fixed a broken thing in my experience.

follow_ups.question: How many drinks in a typical week?
follow_ups.response: Usually zero to three beers, depending on whether there is a game or family cookout.

follow_ups.question: What is your main stress outlet?
follow_ups.response: Making something with my hands or walking before sunset.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I take my prescribed blood pressure medicine, and I use over-the-counter pain medicine carefully for knee or back pain. I do not use marijuana or other drugs. The most recent pain medicine was after a long hike last week; I took ibuprofen with dinner, iced my knee, and skipped the next morning's yard work.

follow_ups.question: Do you worry about pain medicine?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I do not want to rely on it or mess up my stomach, so I use it sparingly.

follow_ups.question: What do you do before taking medicine?
follow_ups.response: Stretch, ice or heat, rest, and see if the pain settles.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: We budget for premiums, prescriptions, and copays like any other fixed expense. I use generic medication, compare pharmacy prices, and try to stay ahead of preventive visits. It is manageable, but it is one reason I keep an emergency fund. One bad dental bill can knock a month sideways.

follow_ups.question: Do you use any discount programs?
follow_ups.response: Yes, pharmacy discount cards sometimes, and I ask for generics.

follow_ups.question: Who handles medical paperwork?
follow_ups.response: Linda is better at forms, but I track the costs in our budget.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am generally pro-vaccine. I got my COVID shots and boosters that were recommended, and I get the flu shot most years. I ask questions, but I am not anti-vaccine.

follow_ups.question: Did you have concerns about COVID vaccines?
follow_ups.response: Some at first because everything felt fast, but I talked to my doctor and decided the risk of getting sick was worse.

follow_ups.question: Does Linda feel the same?
follow_ups.response: Yes, she is even more consistent about flu shots than I am.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: My doctor first, then the pharmacist, and official health department information. I will read news articles, but I do not trust random social media posts or videos from people trying to scare everybody. If it sounds too dramatic, I check it against a medical source.

follow_ups.question: Do friends send you vaccine information?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, and some of it is questionable. I usually do not argue unless it is family.

follow_ups.question: What makes a source credible to you?
follow_ups.response: Clear data, medical training, and willingness to explain risks without selling panic.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: Most of the year I have felt steady, but not without worries. Money, health insurance, and family health sit in the back of my mind. I also had to adjust to being retired because when you are used to being needed for paid work, you can feel a little adrift. The workshops helped a lot because they give me a purpose. I feel best on days when I teach, hike, fix something, or spend time with the grandkids.

follow_ups.question: What time of day is hardest emotionally?
follow_ups.response: Late evening if I start thinking about bills or whether I am doing enough.

follow_ups.question: What helps you reset?
follow_ups.response: A walk, music in the garage, or talking it out with Linda.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: Last fall after my knee swelled up, I had a couple weeks where I felt old in a way I did not like. I had to cancel an ATV ride and ask Brian to help move something I would have moved myself ten years ago. I got grumpy and quiet. Linda finally told me, kindly, that being stubborn was not the same as being strong. That got through to me.

follow_ups.question: What did you do after that conversation?
follow_ups.response: I made a doctor appointment, started exercises, and changed how I plan physical work.

follow_ups.question: Did you tell friends how you felt?
follow_ups.response: A little. Mostly I joked about it, but Mike understood because he has had knee trouble too.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have not been diagnosed with depression or anxiety. I do worry, and I can get down when I feel useless or boxed in by physical limits. But I usually work through it with routine, activity, and talking to Linda. If it got worse, I would talk to a doctor.

follow_ups.question: How do you know when worry is building?
follow_ups.response: I get short-tempered and start overchecking the budget or the calendar.

follow_ups.question: What keeps it from taking over?
follow_ups.response: Having a plan. Even a small list of tasks calms me down.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: The family is mostly okay, but everyone has pressure. The kids are raising children with costs higher than when we were young, and Linda worries about them. We try to be supportive without meddling.

follow_ups.question: What support do you give?
follow_ups.response: Child care here and there, repairs, meals, and listening.

follow_ups.question: Who worries most in the family?
follow_ups.response: Linda carries emotional worry more openly than I do.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I was raised Christian, mostly Protestant, and I still identify that way, but I am not in church every Sunday. Linda and I go a few times a month to a local community church, more often around holidays. My faith is practical: be honest, help your neighbor, do not act like you are better than everyone else, and be grateful for the world you have been given. I also feel something spiritual in the desert, especially early morning near the Superstitions when it is quiet.

follow_ups.question: Are you involved in church activities?
follow_ups.response: Not heavily, but I have helped with maintenance days and a food drive.

follow_ups.question: Did religion shape your upbringing?
follow_ups.response: Yes, in a plain way. We said grace, went to church, and were taught to work hard and treat people decently.

follow_ups.question: Do you pray?
follow_ups.response: Yes, not fancy. Usually short prayers for family health, patience, and guidance.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they use Facebook, Instagram, or other social media to stay connected with the wider world. How about for you? Tell me all about how you use these types of platforms.
transcript.response: I use Facebook some, mostly to see family photos, local events, trail updates, and senior center notices. I am not on Instagram much, and I do not use TikTok. I watch YouTube for repair videos, small engine tips, woodworking tricks, and old music performances. I try not to get dragged into comment fights because that is a waste of a perfectly good afternoon.

follow_ups.question: How often are you on Facebook?
follow_ups.response: Most days for ten or fifteen minutes, usually morning or evening.

follow_ups.question: What YouTube channels do you watch?
follow_ups.response: Mostly practical repair and woodworking channels. I search by problem more than follow personalities.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they use Facebook or Twitter to get (emotional or financial) support during tough times. What about you?
transcript.response: I do not use social media for financial support or personal emotional support. If I am having a hard time, I talk to Linda, family, or a friend directly.

follow_ups.question: Would you post about a crisis?
follow_ups.response: Only if it was something practical, like asking for a recommendation or updating relatives.

follow_ups.question: Do you respond when others ask for help online?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, especially if someone needs a tool, a repair suggestion, or a meal train.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your level of stress, worry, and your emotional coping strategies.
transcript.response: Stress went up with health costs and inflation, but I am coping better by keeping routines. I walk more, plan expenses weekly, and say no to jobs or favors that are too hard on my body.

follow_ups.question: What coping strategy is newest?
follow_ups.response: Evening walks with Linda. It sounds simple, but it helps.

follow_ups.question: What are you trying to stop doing?
follow_ups.response: Stewing quietly instead of saying what is bothering me.

follow_ups.question: Where do you try to save?
follow_ups.response: Eating at home, fixing things myself, combining errands, and watching utility use.

follow_ups.question: Do you track exact categories?

transcript.question_text: Bills can fluctuate over the course of a year. Seasons change, there are holidays and special events, school starts and ends, and so on. Tell me all about how your bills have fluctuated over the past year.
transcript.response: Electric spikes in summer from air conditioning, and gas for the truck goes up when we take road trips or visit family. Holidays raise food and gift spending. Spring can bring yard and home repair costs, especially irrigation parts or roof maintenance after wind.

follow_ups.question: Which season is hardest financially?
follow_ups.response: Summer because of electricity and because you do less free outdoor activity.

follow_ups.question: How do you prepare?
follow_ups.response: I set aside a little each month for seasonal bills.

transcript.question_text: Tell me all about how you coped with any extra expenses in the past months.

follow_ups.question: Was selling woodworking common?

follow_ups.question: What trip did you delay?
follow_ups.response: A short run up toward Sedona.

transcript.question_text: Some people have a savings account, some people save in a different way, and some people say they don't save. How about you?
transcript.response: We have a savings account and retirement accounts, though we are careful about drawing from them. I believe in having an emergency fund because trucks, teeth, and air conditioners do not care what month it is. We are not wealthy, but we have tried to be steady and not carry lifestyle debt.

follow_ups.question: How many months could savings cover?
follow_ups.response: Maybe three months if we tightened up, not counting retirement accounts.

follow_ups.question: Who taught you to save?
follow_ups.response: My parents by example. They did not call it financial planning; they just avoided waste.

transcript.question_text: Some people save for big things, like a home, while others save for a rainy day. How about for you (in the last year)?
transcript.response: This past year our saving has been mostly rainy-day saving: medical, home repairs, vehicle repairs, and a little travel fund. I would like to take Linda back to Monument Valley and maybe White Sands, but I will not put that on a credit card if we cannot pay it off.

follow_ups.question: What is the next planned big expense?
follow_ups.response: Probably air conditioner maintenance or tires for the truck.

follow_ups.question: How do you save for travel?
follow_ups.response: A little cash each month, and we plan road trips instead of flights.

transcript.question_text: Some people have student loans or credit card debt. Others take out loans from family or friends or find other ways of borrowing money. Tell me about all the debts you're paying on right now.
transcript.response: We have the mortgage and one small credit card balance from dental work that we are paying down. No student loans. We do not owe family money, and I try hard not to borrow from relatives.

follow_ups.question: Do you usually carry credit card debt?

follow_ups.question: Any vehicle loans?

transcript.response: We have not missed a bill, but there were a couple months where it was tight enough that we postponed dental work and skipped travel. I count that as not being able to buy something when we wanted or probably needed it. We made it work by trimming extras and using savings carefully.

follow_ups.question: What extras get cut first?
follow_ups.response: Restaurants, trips, hobby purchases, and nonessential tools.

follow_ups.question: Did you ask anyone for help?
follow_ups.response: No, we handled it ourselves.

transcript.question_text: What is or was your occupation? In this occupation, what kind of work do you do and what are the most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: I was a handyman and repairman, with appliance repair, carpentry, small electrical troubleshooting, plumbing fixes, and small engine repair as my main work. A typical job might be fixing a dryer, replacing a garbage disposal, building shelves, repairing a gate, or getting a mower running. The most important duties were diagnosing the problem, doing the work safely, explaining costs honestly, and leaving the place cleaner than I found it. Now I use the same skills teaching workshops and mentoring people who want to fix simple things themselves.

follow_ups.question: What skill made you most valuable?
follow_ups.response: Diagnosis. Anybody can replace parts, but figuring out the real problem saves money.

follow_ups.question: What job did you dislike most?
follow_ups.response: Attic work in summer and anything involving neglected plumbing.

follow_ups.question: What do you enjoy teaching most?
follow_ups.response: Tool safety and basic troubleshooting, because it gives people confidence.

follow_ups.response: Mostly. She liked the routine and knowing people at the school.

follow_ups.response: She could stretch food and hated waste, which I picked up.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: She worked for the local public school district. The cafeteria made breakfast and lunch for students and staff. It was not a business in the usual sense; it was school food service.

follow_ups.question: Was it close to home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, close enough that she knew many families.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever visit her there?
follow_ups.response: Yes, now and then during school events.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes.

follow_ups.question: Was he the main earner?
follow_ups.response: Yes, most of the time.

follow_ups.question: Did he work long hours?
follow_ups.response: Often, especially when repairs backed up.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My dad was an auto mechanic. He diagnosed engine problems, replaced parts, did tune-ups, brakes, belts, and general repairs. His most important skill was listening to a motor and knowing where to start looking.

follow_ups.question: Did he teach you directly?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly by making me watch, hold tools, and try simple tasks.

follow_ups.question: What lesson stayed with you?
follow_ups.response: Do not guess wildly. Observe, test, then fix.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: He worked at a small independent garage. They repaired cars and trucks for local families, ranchers, and small businesses. It was the kind of place where reputation mattered more than advertising.

follow_ups.question: Did that shape your work style?
follow_ups.response: Absolutely. If people trust your work, they come back.

follow_ups.question: Was the garage social too?
follow_ups.response: Yes, people stopped by to talk, get advice, and trade news.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: I hope Linda and I stay healthy enough to remain in our home and keep doing the things that make life feel like ours. I want to expand the senior center workshops and maybe help start a youth apprenticeship program where older tradespeople teach basic repair skills. I would like to write a simple desert living guide: water conservation, native plants, trail safety, tool basics, things like that. I hope to take a few more road trips, especially Monument Valley and White Sands. Mostly I hope my grandkids remember me as someone who showed up and taught them useful things.

follow_ups.question: What would the apprenticeship program look like?
follow_ups.response: Small groups, one evening a week, with safety first and simple projects like shelves, lamps, mower maintenance, and basic home repairs.

follow_ups.question: What would staying independent require?
follow_ups.response: Keeping active, managing money carefully, adapting the house, and asking for help before something becomes a crisis.

follow_ups.question: What road trip do you most want next?
follow_ups.response: Monument Valley with Linda, taking back roads where it is sensible and stopping at local history sites.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value family, usefulness, honesty, independence, and respect for the land. I like people who do what they say, take care of their tools, and help without making a show of it. At this age, I value time more than stuff. A good day is family safe, a problem solved, a little dirt on my boots, and the house quiet at night.

follow_ups.question: What does usefulness mean to you?
follow_ups.response: It means I can make things better in a concrete way, whether that is fixing a fan or teaching a kid to use a drill safely.

follow_ups.question: What do you want passed down?
follow_ups.response: Self-reliance, kindness, patience, and not wasting what you have.
